person_made_it: Three game concepts were invented to be genuinely unlike each other, and then sixty-seven separate sentences were written explaining what design problem each specific image solves; no template and no single prompt produces a Cypriot bread-baking figurine from 600 BCE sitting next to a generated restaurant pass.
emcee_who_is_speaking: A curator writing wall labels, speaking to twelve students who are about to attempt this themselves, which is why every label says what the image is FOR rather than what it looks like.
what_time_of_day_is_this_room: Daylight, a gallery, paper white and quiet, so that three boards with violently different palettes can hang in the same space without any of them winning.
did_the_click_pay_me: Yes: the six words are in the first screen, and the first board's full argument is visible before any scrolling decision has to be made.
works_for_the_recipient: It collapses to one column at 390px, needs no JavaScript, prints, lazy-loads sixty-seven images, and every one of the thirty-eight Met links was confirmed in a real browser after curl was blocked by bot protection.
taught_me_something: That measuring a mood board's palette from its own pixels exposes something a student would never admit: the historical reference plates drag every board toward aged paper, so a board's stated tone and its actual color can disagree by a lot.
told_me_the_truth: Yes, three times over: the palette strips are split into look and reference instead of averaged into a flattering single strip, the generated plates print their full prompts, and the page names the one Met image that 404s and what was used instead.
weakest: The three concepts are mine rather than a real team's, so the boards are more internally consistent than any actual first team's will be in week three; the page would teach more if one board were deliberately left with the seams a real group leaves.
